The viral nucleoprotein is a key component of the virus, along with the phosphoprotein (P), matrix protein (M), glycoprotein (G), and the viral RNA polymerase (L). The RNA genome of the virus encodes these five genes in a highly conserved order. To enter cells, trimeric spikes on the exterior of the virus interact with a specific cell receptor, most likely the acetylcholine receptor. The cellular membrane pinches in a process known as pinocytosis, allowing entry of the virus into the cell by way of an endosome. The virus then uses the acidic environment of that endosome and binds to its membrane simultaneously, releasing its five proteins and single-strand RNA into the cytoplasm.

Once within a muscle or nerve cell, the virus undergoes replication. The L protein then transcribes five mRNA strands and a positive strand of RNA all from the original negative strand RNA using free nucleotides in the cytoplasm. These five mRNA strands are then translated into the corresponding proteins.

As for the rhetoric textbook, it is "The twofold copia of words and arguments in a double commentary," also known as De duplici copia verborum ac rerum commentarii duo, written by Erasmus. It was the most often printed rhetoric textbook written in the renaissance, with 168 editions between 1512 and 1580. The first part of the book is about verborum (words) and includes 147 variations on "Your letter pleased me very much," and 203 variations on "Always, as long as I live, I shall remember you." The second part of the book is about rerum (arguments) to learn critical thinking and advocacy. Erasmus advised students to practice the rhetorical techniques of copiousness by writing letters to each other arguing both sides of an issue. Other works by Erasmus include Opuscula plutarchi (1514), and Apophthegmata Patrum (1500).
